catalog_quote: [1936: 411] (1) The relationship between dynamic stress and 'musical' pitch in the south Dravidian speeches requires to be experimentally investigated. So far as I can see, accent in these speeches is constituted of both elements. The accent-marks (strong, medium,) given in this essay only symbolise a perceptible rise in stress or in pitch. Generally speaking, accent falls on the root-syllables of native words when separately uttered. In connected speech, two degrees of accent may be demarcated thus roughly: the strong accent which falls on the initial root syllables of important words of each breath-group, and a less strong accent on the root-syllables of other emphatic words in the breath-group. Statements or exclamations expressive of strong feelings of course involve different degrees and varieties of accent in which pitch or intonation completely submerges the stress element ... [1932: 906 n. 1-907] Word-accent and sentence-accent exist in the enunciation of Tuḷu, as in the other south Dravidian speeches, though the precise character of this accent (i.e. whether it is dynamic stress or tonal pitch or a combination of the two) remains to be determined with the help of scientific instruments. ... So far as single words of two or more syllables are concerned, the primary accent generally falls on the root-syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tulu is not in the catalog. The single title hit, Radhakrishna 2005 'Tulu Prosody: A critical study' (Kannur Univ. Ph.D., Kannada), was downloaded in full from Shodhganga (hdl 10603/110069) and read from page images: it is a study of verse metre (chandas), silent on word stress; its section 3.10 'ಸ್ಟ್ ಎಂಬ ಧ್ವನಿಮಾ' concerns the Old-Tulu alveolar consonant 'sṭ', not stress. Two further open Shodhganga theses were downloaded and read: Rama 1978 'Structural Description of Tulu' (Kerala; = Glottolog's Rama 2017 Kasaragod Tulu) has a 'Stress' section (p. 85) treating stress only as normal-vs-emphatic vocal qualifiers with no placement rule, and Kekunnaya 1990 'Comparative Study of Tulu Dialects' (Mangalore) has no suprasegmental section at all. The best first-hand statements remain Ramaswami Aiyar 1936 p. 411 (accent on the root = initial root syllable of native words, weak, stress-plus-pitch) and 1932 pp. 906-907 (primary accent generally on the root syllable), both read from saved page images. Unread and worth acquiring: Shetty 2001 Comprehensive Grammar of Tulu (high; secondary citation says first syllable usually stressed), Bhat 1967 and Bhatt 1971 (medium; snippets only, HathiTrust search-only). with updated.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (559 pp., DLI scan, no text layer) and rendered PDF page 432 fresh: it carries printed page number 411, heading 'Short notes regarding the sounds', note (1). The full quoted passage ('The relationship between dynamic stress and 'musical' pitch.. a less strong accent on the root-syllables of other emphatic words in the breath-group.') is on that page verbatim, punctuation included ('may be demarcated thus roughly:'); the saved page image shows the same. The djvu scanned ( lines 20091-20101) differs only by scanned slips ('maybe', 'roughly;'). The accent-mark convention is indeed on p. 410 fn. (1) (bars above = primary, below = secondary). Article header confirmed at the scanned…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (a mix of stress and pitch, weak by the author's own acoustic impression) falls on the root syllable of native words, which in Tulu/Dravidian is the word-initial syllable; the author himself says 'initial root syllables'. An equally faithful label would be morphologically determined, but since Dravidian roots are word-initial the two coincide. Nothing is said about contrastiveness; the companion 1932 text (BSOS 6: 906 n.1, 907) says 'so far as single words of two or more syllables are concerned, the primary accent generally falls on the root-syllable' and that the nature of the accent (dynamic stress vs pitch) is undetermined.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Phrase-level only: 'a less strong accent on the root-syllables of other emphatic words in the breath-group'. In the transcribed texts a bar above marks primary and a bar below secondary accent (p. 410 fn. 1; 1932: 907), but no word-internal secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Exclamations/statements of strong feeling: 'pitch or intonation completely submerges the stress element' (p. 411). Grammatical accent on endings: [ʌ] 'in unaccented syllables has the value of [a]; but sometimes when for certain grammatical differentiations, [ʌ] has to receive a little stress or accent' e.g. 2pl. vs 3pl. tense endings (p. 412). Sentence accent is 'governed by the psychological importance of the particular word' (1932: 907).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly distinguishes single words 'when separately uttered' (citation form) from connected speech / breath-groups (sentence accent). Accent described as perceptible rise in stress or pitch, 'far less strong' than Hindi stress (1932: 906 n.1).
new_statements.identity_note: Ramaswami Aiyar's data are Tulu of the Udipi / South Kanara area (informants such as Sridhar Sarma of Udipi), covering both the Brahmins' (Shivalli) dialect and the common 'folk-speech'; the 1936 remark is made for 'these passages' generally, not for one dialect. No separate Glottolog dialect code; the language-level code tulu1258 applies.

new_statements.reading: Word accent in Tulu falls on the root syllable, which the author identifies as the initial (root) syllable of native words; it is a weak accent made of both stress and pitch (the 1932 footnote adds that the primary accent 'generally falls on the root-syllable' of polysyllabic words and that its dynamic-vs-tonal nature is undetermined). Reads as fixed initial stress, impressionistic, with sentence-level prominence governed by pragmatic importance. Nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title gives a placement rule that is more explicit or more recent; Shetty 2001 (unread) reportedly says 'first syllable is usually stressed'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement only: stress is not phonemic in any Dravidian language; it normally falls on the initial syllable of the word, whether that syllable is short or long; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (a phonetic weight effect, not a placement rule). Tulu is not named in the statement; the Tulu entry on p. 24 says nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated for Tulu. The only related remark is that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Tulu. 'Normally' hedges the family-wide claim; p. 28 adds that short vowels in non-root syllables 'in unaccented position' tend to be lost.
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti 2003 p. 24 describes Tulu (Tuluva) of Dakshina Kannada district (Karnataka) and Kasaragod taluk (Kerala) with a four-way dialect division North/South x Brahmin/Common; the p. 27 stress statement is family-wide and names no dialect. The catalog's existing statements rest on Ramaswami Aiyar's Udupi Brahmin + folk speech = tulu1258.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Tulu fixed-unreviewed, initial: initial stress, from Ramaswami Aiyar 1936 p. 411 'accent falls on the root-syllables of native words' = initial root syllable) and identical to existing statement no. 3 held by the project, which is this very sentence (p. 27, verified). It adds, at family level, that stress is non-phonemic and that non-initial long vowels carry extra loudness; it is not a Tulu-specific observation, so it corroborates rather than independently establishes the Tulu coding.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide typological statement (Tulu is one of the 26 languages covered, SD I no. 5, but is not named in this sentence): stress is not phonemic anywhere in Dravidian; phonetic stress (loudness) normally falls on the word-initial syllable whether that syllable is short or long; a long vowel in a non-initial syllable is louder than short vowels; non-root (= unaccented) syllables tend to lose short vowels. No Tulu-specific stress statement is in the held pages; whether sec. 2.4 (pp. 58-60) says anything about Tulu could not be checked (earlier Google Books snippet queries for Tulu+stress in this volume returned only the p. 27 sentence).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated as such; only 'A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (p. 27), i.e. added prominence on non-initial long vowels, not called secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none in the held pages (the statement is hedged with 'Normally').
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti 2003 treats Tulu as South Dravidian I language no. 5 (pp. 23-24: Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts of Karnataka and Kasaragod, Kerala; Brahmin vs common Tulu, regional dialects NB/NC/SB/SC) = Glottolog tulu1258; the stress sentence quoted is a family-wide typological statement, not a description of any Tulu variety. The catalog source (Ramaswami Aiyar 1936/1932) describes Udipi Brahmin Tulu and folk speech of South Canara.

sources.quote: Loudness and force of the speech are known as vocal qualifiers. In this dialect we notice two kinds of vocal qualifiers i.e. primary and secondary. The usual talk with normal speed is always identified as primary vocal qualifier. The extra-ordinary talk like extra short and extra long which are responsible in the meaning change of a particular speech, and exclamation come under secondary vocal qualifier. The usage of secondary vocal qualifier is very limited. [...] But within a word either one of these will occur.
sources.locator: ch. 1 Phonology, sec. 1.6 Suprasegmental Phonemes (thesis p. 84) and sec. 1.6.2 Stress (thesis p. 85) = pdf pages 31-32 of
sources.note: Treats 'stress' as expressive vocal qualifiers (normal vs emphatic), phonemic together with juncture, pitch (4 levels) and intonation; gives no rule of word-stress position. In its examples the primary mark sits on the first syllable of most words (àaye bàtte 'he came'; ònji, òri, ìtte) but on a non-initial syllable in uurùdu, aràse, naràmaani. Silent on a placement rule.
